entries.666d5c7cfaa757818ada3af0a217dc788df284c8: <div sID="gen3176" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="24" osisID="Num.24" sID="Num.24"/> <div eID="gen3176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3177" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen3178" type="x-p"/> This chapter continues and concludes the history of the defeat of the counsels of Balak and Balaam against Israel, not by might, nor by power, but by the Spirit of the Lord of hosts; and as great an instance it is of God's power over the children of men, and his favour towards his own children, as any of the victories recorded in the book of the wars of the Lord. What preparation was made the third time for the cursing of Israel we read of in the close of the foregoing chapter. In this chapter we are told, I. What the blessing was into which that intended curse was turned, <reference osisRef="Num.24.1-Num.24.9">ver. 1-9</reference>. II. How Balak dismissed Balaam from his service thereupon, <reference osisRef="Num.24.10-Num.24.13">ver. 10-13</reference>. III. The predictions Balaam left behind him concerning Israel, and some of the neighbouring nations, <reference osisRef="Num.24.14-Num.24.25">ver. 14</reference>, &c.
entries.7862ab85f618020a8b06e7435e554ae20df74f15: <div eID="gen3178" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen3177" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Balaam Blesses Israel a Third Time. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1452.)</title> <div sID="gen3179" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And when Balaam saw that it pleased the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> to bless Israel, he went not, as at other times, to seek for enchantments, but he set his face toward the wilderness. 2 And Balaam lifted up his eyes, and he saw Israel abiding <hi type="italic">in his tents</hi> according to their tribes; and the spirit of God came upon him. 3 And he took up his parable, and said, Balaam the son of Beor hath said, and the man whose eyes are open hath said: 4 He hath said, which heard the words of God, which saw the vision of the Almighty, falling <hi type="italic">into a trance,</hi> but having his eyes open: 5 How goodly are thy tents, O Jacob, <hi type="italic">and</hi> thy tabernacles, O Israel! 6 As the valleys are they spread forth, as gardens by the river's side, as the trees of lign aloes which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath planted, <hi type="italic">and</hi> as cedar trees beside the waters. 7 He shall pour the water out of his buckets, and his seed <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> in many waters, and his king shall be higher than Agag, and his kingdom shall be exalted. 8 God brought him forth out of Egypt; he hath as it were the strength of an unicorn: he shall eat up the nations his enemies, and shall break their bones, and pierce <hi type="italic">them</hi> through with his arrows. 9 He couched, he lay down as a lion, and as a great lion: who shall stir him up? Blessed <hi type="italic">is</hi> he that blesseth thee, and cursed <hi type="italic">is</hi> he that curseth thee. <div eID="gen3179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3180" type="x-p"/> The blessing itself which Balaam here pronounces upon Israel is much the same with the two we had in the foregoing chapter; but the introduction to it is different. <div eID="gen3180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3181" type="x-p"/> I. The method of proceeding here varies much in several instances. 1. Balaam laid aside the enchantments which he had hitherto depended on, used no spells, or charms, or magic arts, finding they did him no service; it was to no purpose to deal with the devil for a curse, when it was plain that God was determined immovably to bless, <reference osisRef="Num.24.1">v. 1</reference>. Sooner or later God will convince men of their folly in seeking after lying vanities, which cannot profit. To what purpose should he seek for enchantment? He knew that God was out of the reach of them. 2. He did not now retire into a solitary place as before, but set his face directly towards the wilderness where Israel lay encamped; and, since there is no remedy, but they must be blessed, he will design nothing else, but will submit by compulsion. 3. Now <hi type="italic">the Spirit of God came upon him,</hi> that is, the Spirit of prophecy, as upon Saul to prevent him from taking David, <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.23">1 Sam. xix. 23</reference>. He spoke not his own sense, but the language of the Spirit that came upon him. 4. He used a different preface now from what he had used before (<reference osisRef="Num.24.3-Num.24.4">v. 3, 4</reference>), much like that of David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.1-2Sam.23.3">2 Sam. xxiii. 1-3</reference>), yet savouring very much (as some think) of pride and vain-glory, taking all the praise of this prophecy to himself, and magnifying himself as one of the cabinet-council of heaven. Two things he boasts of:—(1.) The favour God did him in making known himself to him. He <hi type="italic">heard the words of God, and saw the vision of the Almighty.</hi> God himself had met him and spoken to him (<reference osisRef="Num.23.16">ch. xxiii. 16</reference>), and with this he was greatly puffed up. Paul speaks with humility of his visions and revelations (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.1">2 Cor. xii. 1</reference>), but Balaam speaks of his with pride. (2.) His own power to receive and bear those revelations. He fell into a trance indeed, as other prophets did, but he had his eyes open. This he mentions twice; but the words in the original are not the same. The <hi type="italic">man whose eyes were shut,</hi> some think it may be read so (<reference osisRef="Num.24.3-Num.24.9">v. 3-9</reference>), but now <hi type="italic">having his eyes open,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.24.4">v. 4</reference>. When he attempted to curse Israel, he owns, he was in a mistake, but now he began to see his error, and yet still he remained blinded by covetousness and ambition, those foolish and hurtful lusts. Note, [1.] Those that oppose God and his people will sooner or later be made to see themselves wretchedly deceived. [2.] Many have their eyes open that have not their hearts open, are enlightened, but not sanctified; and that knowledge which puffs men up with pride will but serve to light them to hell, whither many go with their eyes open. <div eID="gen3181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3182" type="x-p"/> II. Yet the blessing is for substance the same with those before. Several things he admires in Israel:— <div eID="gen3182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3183" type="x-p"/> 1. Their beauty (<reference osisRef="Num.24.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">How goodly are thy tents, O Jacob!</hi> Though they dwelt not in stately palaces, but in coarse and homely tents, and these, no doubt, sadly weather-beaten, yet Balaam sees a beauty in those tents, because of their admirable order, according to their tribes, <reference osisRef="Num.24.2">v. 2</reference>. Nothing recommends religion more to the good opinion of those that look upon it at a distance than the unity and harmony of its professors, <reference osisRef="Ps.133.1">Ps. cxxxiii. 1</reference>. The amiableness of this people, and the great reputation they should gain among their neighbours, are compared (<reference osisRef="Num.24.6">v. 6</reference>) to the beauty and sweetness of fruitful valleys and fine gardens, flourishing trees and fragrant spices. Note, Those whose eyes are open see the saints on the earth to be excellent ones, and their delight is accordingly in them. <hi type="italic">The righteous,</hi> doubtless, <hi type="italic">is more excellent than his neighbour.</hi> They are <hi type="italic">trees which the Lord has planted;</hi> that is their excellency. The branches of righteousness are the planting of the Lord. See <reference osisRef="Hos.14.5-Hos.14.7">Hos. xiv. 5-7</reference>. <div eID="gen3183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3184" type="x-p"/> 2. Their fruitfulness and increase. This may be intended by those similitudes (<reference osisRef="Num.24.6">v. 6</reference>) of the valleys, gardens, and trees, as well as by those expressions (<reference osisRef="Num.24.7">v. 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">He shall pour the water out of his buckets;</hi> that is, God shall water them with his blessing like rain from heaven, and then his <hi type="italic">seed shall be in many waters.</hi> Compare <reference osisRef="Hos.2.23">Hos. ii. 23</reference>, <hi type="italic">I will sow her unto me in the earth.</hi> And waters are in scripture put for <hi type="italic">peoples, and multitudes, and nations.</hi> This has been fulfilled in the wonderful increase of that nation and their vast multitude even in their dispersion. <div eID="gen3184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3185" type="x-p"/> 3. Their honour and advancement. As the multitude of the people is the honour of the prince, so the magnificence of the prince is the honour of the people; Balaam therefore foretells that their <hi type="italic">king shall be higher than Agag.</hi> Agag, it is probable, was the most potent monarch in those parts; Balaam knew of none more considerable than he was; he rose above the rest of his neighbours. But Balaam foretells that Israel's chief commander, who, after Moses, was Joshua, should be more great and honourable than ever Agag was, and make a far better figure in history. Saul, their first king, triumphed over Agag, though, it is said, <hi type="italic">he came delicately.</hi> <div eID="gen3185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3186" type="x-p"/> 4. Their power and victory, <reference osisRef="Num.24.8">v. 8</reference>. (1.) He looks back upon what they had done, or rather what had been done for them: <hi type="italic">God brought them forth out of Egypt;</hi> this he had spoken of before, <reference osisRef="Num.23.22">ch. xxiii. 22</reference>. The wonders that attended their deliverance out of Egypt contributed more to their honour, and the terror of their adversaries, than any thing else, <reference osisRef="Josh.2.10">Josh. ii. 10</reference>. He that brought them out of Egypt will not fail to bring them into Canaan, for, <hi type="italic">as for God, his work is perfect.</hi> (2.) He looks down upon their present strength. Israel hath, as it were, <hi type="italic">the strength of a unicorn,</hi> of which creature it is said (<reference osisRef="Job.39.9-Job.39.10">Job xxxix. 9, 10</reference>), <hi type="italic">Will he be willing to serve thee, or abide by thy crib? Canst thou bind him with his band in the furrow?</hi> "No, Israel is too powerful to be checked or held in by my curses or thy armies." (3.) He looks forward to their future conquests: <hi type="italic">He shall eat up the nations his enemies;</hi> that is, "he shall not only destroy and devour them as easily and irresistibly as a lion does his prey, but he shall himself be strengthened, and fattened, and enriched, by their spoils." <div eID="gen3186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3187" type="x-p"/> 5. Their courage and security: <hi type="italic">He lay down as a lion, as a great lion,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.24.9">v. 9</reference>. Now he does so in the plains of Moab, and asks no leave of the king of Moab, nor is he in fear of him; shortly will he do so in Canaan. When he has torn his prey, he will take his repose, <hi type="italic">quiet from the fear of evil,</hi> and bid defiance to all his neighbours; for who shall stir up a sleeping lion? It is observed of lions (as the learned bishop Patrick takes notice here) that they do not retire into places of shelter to sleep, but lie down any where, knowing that none dares meddle with them: thus secure were Israel in Canaan, chiefly in the days of David and Solomon; and thus is <hi type="italic">the righteous bold as a lion</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.28.1">Prov. xxviii. 1</reference>), not to assault others, but to repose themselves, because <hi type="italic">God maketh them to dwell in safety,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.4.8">Ps. iv. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen3187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3188" type="x-p"/> 6. Their interest, and influence upon their neighbours. Their friends, and those in alliance with them, were happy: <hi type="italic">Blessed is he that blesseth thee;</hi> those that do them any kindness will certainly fare the better for it. But their enemies, and those in arms against them, were certainly miserable: <hi type="italic">Cursed is he that curseth thee;</hi> those that do them any injury do it at their peril; for God takes what is done to them, whether good or evil, as done to himself. Thus he confirms the blessing of Abraham (<reference osisRef="Gen.12.3">Gen. xii. 3</reference>), and speaks as if <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> he did at this time bless Israel, and not curse them, because he desired to share in the blessing of Israel's friends and dreaded the curse on Israel's enemies.
entries.4184cbeb67077b7e7714ad41142a30d54b35e857: <div eID="gen3188" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Balak's Remonstrance. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1452.)</title> <div sID="gen3189" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> And Balak's anger was kindled against Balaam, and he smote his hands together: and Balak said unto Balaam, I called thee to curse mine enemies, and, behold, thou hast altogether blessed <hi type="italic">them</hi> these three times. 11 Therefore now flee thou to thy place: I thought to promote thee unto great honour; but, lo, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath kept thee back from honour. 12 And Balaam said unto Balak, Spake I not also to thy messengers which thou sentest unto me, saying, 13 If Balak would give me his house full of silver and gold, I cannot go beyond the commandment of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , to do <hi type="italic">either</hi> good or bad of mine own mind; <hi type="italic">but</hi> what the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> saith, that will I speak? 14 And now, behold, I go unto my people: come <hi type="italic">therefore, and</hi> I will advertise thee what this people shall do to thy people in the latter days. <div eID="gen3189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3190" type="x-p"/> We have here the conclusion of this vain attempt to curse Israel, and the total abandonment of it. 1. Balak made the worst of it. He broke out into a rage against Balaam (<reference osisRef="Num.24.10">v. 10</reference>), expressed both in words and gesture the highest degree of vexation at the disappointment; he smote his hands together, for indignation, to see all his measures thus broken, and his project baffled. He charged Balaam with putting upon him the basest affront and cheat imaginable: "<hi type="italic">I called thee to curse my enemies,</hi> and thou hast shown thyself in league with them, and in their interests, for thou hast <hi type="italic">blessed them these three times,</hi> though, by appointing the altars to be built and sacrifices to be offered, thou madest be believe thou wouldest certainly curse them." Hereupon he forbade him his presence, expelled him his country, upbraided him with the preferments he had designed to bestow upon him, but now would not (<reference osisRef="Num.24.11">v. 11</reference>): "<hi type="italic">The Lord hath kept thee back from honour.</hi> See what thou gettest by pleasing the Lord, instead of pleasing me; thou has hindered thy preferment by it." Thus those who are any way losers by their duty are commonly upbraided with it, as fools, for preferring it before their interest in the world. Whereas, if Balaam had been voluntary and sincere in his adherence to the word of the Lord, though he lost the honour Balak designed him by it, God would have made that loss up to him abundantly to his advantage. 2. Balaam made the best if it. (1.) He endeavours to excuse the disappointment. And a very good excuse he has for it, that God restrained him from saying what he would have said, and constrained him to say what he would not; and that this was what Balak ought not to be displeased at, not only because he could not help it, but because he had told Balak before what he must depend upon, <reference osisRef="Num.24.12-Num.24.13">v. 12, 13</reference>. Balak could not say that he had cheated him, since he had given him fair notice of the check he found himself under. (2.) He endeavours to atone for it, <reference osisRef="Num.24.14">v. 14</reference>. Though he cannot do what Balak would have him do, yet, [1.] He will gratify his curiosity with some predictions concerning the nations about him. It is natural to us to be pleased with prophecy, and with this he hopes to pacify the angry prince. [2.] He will satisfy him with an assurance that, whatever this formidable people should do to his people, it should not be till the latter days; so that he, for his part, needed not to fear any mischief or molestation from them; the <hi type="italic">vision was for a great while to come,</hi> but in his days there should be peace. [3.] He will put him into a method of doing Israel a mischief without the ceremonies of enchantment and execration. This seems to be implied in that word: <hi type="italic">I will advertise thee;</hi> for it properly signifies, <hi type="italic">I will counsel thee.</hi> What the counsel was is not set down here, because it was given privately, but we are told afterwards what it was, <reference osisRef="Num.31.16">ch. xxxi. 16</reference>. He counselled him to entice the Israelites to idolatry, <reference osisRef="Rev.2.14">Rev. ii. 14</reference>. Since he could not have leave from God to curse them, he puts him in a way of getting help from the devil to tempt them. <hi type="italic">Flectere si nequeo superos, Acheronta movebo—If I cannot move heaven, I will solicit hell.</hi>
entries.efe72d684618c6ec2aff41a3c673ec48bde24de7: <div eID="gen3190" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Balaam's Prophecy. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1452.)</title> <div sID="gen3191" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> And he took up his parable, and said, Balaam the son of Beor hath said, and the man whose eyes are open hath said: 16 He hath said, which heard the words of God, and knew the knowledge of the most High, <hi type="italic">which</hi> saw the vision of the Almighty, falling <hi type="italic">into a trance,</hi> but having his eyes open: 17 I shall see him, but not now: I shall behold him, but not nigh: there shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel, and shall smite the corners of Moab, and destroy all the children of Sheth. 18 And Edom shall be a possession, Seir also shall be a possession for his enemies; and Israel shall do valiantly. 19 Out of Jacob shall come he that shall have dominion, and shall destroy him that remaineth of the city. 20 And when he looked on Amalek, he took up his parable, and said, Amalek <hi type="italic">was</hi> the first of the nations; but his latter end <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> that he perish for ever. 21 And he looked on the Kenites, and took up his parable, and said, Strong is thy dwellingplace, and thou puttest thy nest in a rock. 22 Nevertheless the Kenite shall be wasted, until Asshur shall carry thee away captive. 23 And he took up his parable, and said, Alas, who shall live when God doeth this! 24 And ships <hi type="italic">shall come</hi> from the coast of Chittim, and shall afflict Asshur, and shall afflict Eber, and he also shall perish for ever. 25 And Balaam rose up, and went and returned to his place: and Balak also went his way. <div eID="gen3191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3192" type="x-p"/> The office of prophets was both to bless and to prophesy in the name of the Lord. Balaam, as a prophet, per force had blessed Israel; here he foretells future events. <div eID="gen3192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3193" type="x-p"/> I. His preface is much the same as that, <reference osisRef="Num.24.3-Num.24.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. He personates a true prophet admirably well, God permitting and directing him to do so, because, whatever he was, the prophecy itself was a true prophecy. He boasts, 1. That his <hi type="italic">eyes are open</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.24.15">v. 15</reference>), for prophets were <hi type="italic">in old time called seers</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.9">1 Sam. ix. 9</reference>), because they must speak what they had seen, and therefore, before they opened their lips, it was necessary that they should have their eyes open. 2. That he has <hi type="italic">heard the words of God,</hi> which many do that do not heed them, nor hear God in them. 3. That he <hi type="italic">knew the knowledge of the Most High;</hi> this is added here. A man may be full of the knowledge of God and yet utterly destitute of the grace of God, may receive the truth in the light of it and yet be a stranger to the love of it. 4. That <hi type="italic">he saw the vision of the Almighty,</hi> but not so as to be <hi type="italic">changed into the same image.</hi> He calls God the <hi type="italic">Most High,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">Almighty;</hi> no man could speak more honourably of him, nor seem to put a greater value upon his acquaintance with him, and yet he had no true fear of him, love to him, or faith in him, so far may a man go towards heaven, and yet come short. <div eID="gen3193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3194" type="x-p"/> II. Here is his prophecy concerning him that should be the crown and glory of his people Israel, who is, 1. David in the type, who <hi type="italic">not now,</hi> not quickly, but in process of time, should <hi type="italic">smite the corners of Moab.</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.24.17">v. 17</reference>), and take possession of Mount Seir, and under whom the forces of Israel should <hi type="italic">do valiantly,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.24.18">v. 18</reference>. This was fulfilled when David smote Moab, and <hi type="italic">measured them with a line,</hi> so that <hi type="italic">the Moabites became David's servants,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.2">2 Sam. viii. 2</reference>. And at the same time the Edomites likewise were brought into obedience to Israel, <reference osisRef="Num.24.14">v. 14</reference>. But, 2. Our Lord Jesus, the promised Messiah, is chiefly pointed at in the antitype, and of him it is an illustrious prophecy; it was the will of God that notice should thus be given of his coming, a great while before, not only to the people of the Jews, but to other nations, because his gospel and kingdom were to extend themselves so far beyond the borders of the land of Israel. It is here foretold, (1.) That while: "<hi type="italic">I shall see him, but not now;</hi> I do see him in vision, but at a very great distance, through the interposing space of 1500 years at least." Or understand it thus:—Balaam, a wicked man, shall see Christ, but shall not see him nigh, nor see him as Job, who saw him <hi type="italic">as his Redeemer,</hi> and saw him for himself, <reference osisRef="Job.19.25">Job xix. 25, 27</reference>. When he comes in the clouds <hi type="italic">every eye shall see him,</hi> but many will see him (as the rich man in hell saw Abraham) <hi type="italic">afar off.</hi> (2.) That he shall come out of Jacob, and Israel, as a star and a sceptre, the former denoting his glory and lustre, and the <hi type="italic">bright and morning star,</hi> the latter his power and authority; it is <hi type="italic">he that shall have dominion.</hi> Perhaps this prophecy of Balaam (one of the children of the east) concerning a star that should arise out of Jacob, as the indication of a sceptre arising in Israel, being preserved by a tradition of that country, gave occasion to the wise men, who were of the east too, upon the sight of an unusual star over the land of Judea, to enquire for him that was <hi type="italic">born king of the Jews,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.2.2">Matt. ii. 2</reference>. (3.) That his kingdom shall be universal, and victorious over all opposition, which was typified by David's victories over Moab and Edom. But the Messiah shall destroy, or, as some read it, <hi type="italic">shall rule over, all the children of Seth.</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.24.17">v. 17</reference>), that is, all the children of men, who descend from Seth, the son of Adam, the descendants of the rest of Adam's sons being cut off by the deluge. Christ shall be king, not only of Jacob and Israel, but of all the world; so that all the children of Seth shall be either governed by his golden sceptre or dashed in pieces by his iron rod. He shall set up a universal rule, authority, and power, of his own, and shall put down all opposing rule, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.24">1 Cor. xv. 24</reference>. He shall <hi type="italic">unwall all the children of Seth;</hi> so some read it. He shall take down all their defences and carnal confidences, so that they shall either admit his government or lie open to his judgments. (4.) That his Israel shall do valiantly; the subjects of Christ, animated by his might, shall maintain a spiritual war with the powers of darkness, and be more than conquerors. <hi type="italic">The people that do know their God shall be strong, and do exploits,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.11.32">Dan. xi. 32</reference>. <div eID="gen3194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3195" type="x-p"/> III. Here is his prophecy concerning the Amalekites and Kenites, part of whose country, it is probable, he had now in view. 1. The Amalekites were now the <hi type="italic">chief of the nations</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.24.20">v. 20</reference>), therefore Agag was spoken of (<reference osisRef="Num.24.7">v. 7</reference>) as an eminent prince, and they were the first that engaged Israel when they came out of Egypt; but the time will come when that nation, as great as it looks now, will be totally ruined and rooted out: <hi type="italic">His latter end shall be that he perish for ever.</hi> Here Balaam confirms that doom of Amalek which Moses had read (<reference osisRef="Exod.15.14">Exod. xv. 14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.15.16">16</reference>), where God had sworn that he would have <hi type="italic">perpetual war with Amalek.</hi> Note, Those whom God is at war with will certainly perish for ever; for when God judges he will overcome. 2. The Kenites were now the securest of the nations; their situation was such as that nature was their engineer, and had strongly fortified them: "<hi type="italic">Thou puttest thy nest</hi> (like the eagle) <hi type="italic">in a rock,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.24.21">v. 21</reference>. Thou thinkest thyself safe, and yet the <hi type="italic">Kenites shall be wasted</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.24.22">v. 22</reference>) and gradually brought to decay, till they be carried away captive by the Assyrians," which was done at the captivity of the ten tribes. Note, Bodies politic, like natural bodies, though of the strongest constitutions, will gradually decay, and come to ruin at last; even a nest in a rock will be no perpetual security. <div eID="gen3195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3196" type="x-p"/> IV. Here is a prophecy that looks as far forward as the Greeks and Romans, for theirs is supposed to be meant by the <hi type="italic">coast of Chittim,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.24.24">v. 24</reference>. <div eID="gen3196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3197" type="x-p"/> 1. The introduction to this parable; this article of his prophecy is very observable (<reference osisRef="Num.24.23">v. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">Alas! who shall live when God doeth this?</hi> Here he acknowledges all the revolutions of states and kingdoms to be the Lord's doing: <hi type="italic">God doeth this;</hi> whoever are the instruments, he is the supreme director. But he speaks mournfully concerning them, and has a very melancholy prospect of these events: <hi type="italic">Who shall live?</hi> Either, (1.) These events are so distant, and so far off to come, that it is hard to say <hi type="italic">who shall live till they come;</hi> but, whoever shall live to see them, there will be amazing turns. Or, (2.) They will be so dismal, and make such desolations, that scarcely any will escape or be left alive; who shall live when death rides in triumph? <reference osisRef="Rev.6.8">Rev. vi. 8</reference>. Those that live then will be as brands plucked out of the fire, and will have their lives given them as a prey. God fit us for the worst of times! <div eID="gen3197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3198" type="x-p"/> 2. The prophecy itself is observable. Both Greece and Italy lie much upon the sea, and therefore their armies were sent forth mostly in ships. Now he seems here to foretell, (1.) That the forces of the Grecians should humble and bring down the Assyrians, who were united with the Persians, which was fulfilled when the eastern country was overcome, or overrun rather, by Alexander. (2.) That theirs and the Roman forces should afflict the Hebrews, or Jews, who were called <hi type="italic">the children of Eber;</hi> this was fulfilled in part when the Grecian empire was oppressive to the Jewish nation, but chiefly when the Roman empire ruined it and put a period to it. But, (3.) That Chittim, that is, the Roman empire, in which the Grecian was at length swallowed up, should itself perish for ever, when the stone cut out of the mountain without hands shall consume all these kingdoms, and particularly the <hi type="italic">feet of iron and clay,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.2.34">Dan. ii. 34</reference>. Thus (says Dr. Lightfoot) Balaam, instead of cursing the church, curses Amalek the first, and Rome the last, enemy of the church. And <hi type="italic">so let all thy enemies perish, O Lord!</hi>  <chapter eID="Num.24"/> <div eID="gen3198" type="x-p"/>

entries.4c0202a3af7ae119e51c659151ade66e22cc8b40: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1520"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 24</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Num.24.1-Num.24.25">Nu 24:1-25</reference>. Balaam Foretells Israel's Happiness.</title> <div sID="gen2038" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1520"/><hi type="bold">1. to seek for--</hi>that is, to use enchantments. His experience on the two former occasions [Nu 23:3, 15] had taught him that these superstitious accompaniments of his worship were useless, and therefore he now simply looked towards the camp of Israel, either with a secret design to curse them, or to await the divine afflatus. <div eID="gen2038" type="x-p"/>
entries.936b9aa3ef2035882b6d8c26dc3189155da05590: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1521"/><div sID="gen2039" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1521"/><hi type="bold">2. he saw Israel abiding in his tents according to their tribes--</hi>that is, in the orderly distribution of the camp (<reference osisRef="Num.2.1-Num.2.34">Nu 2:1-34</reference>).<div eID="gen2039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2040" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the spirit of God came upon him--</hi>Before the regular ministry of the prophets was instituted, God made use of various persons as the instruments through whom He revealed His will, and Balaam was one of these (<reference osisRef="Deut.23.5">De 23:5</reference>). <div eID="gen2040" type="x-p"/>
entries.792279e9e4fb6ed2b19904ee49210d46e95b4d5a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1522"/><div sID="gen2041" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1522"/><hi type="bold">3. the man whose eyes are open--</hi>that is, a seer (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.9">1Sa 9:9</reference>), a prophet, to whom the visioned future was disclosed--sometimes when falling into a sleep (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.12-Gen.15.15">Ge 15:12-15</reference>), frequently into "a trance." <div eID="gen2041" type="x-p"/>
entries.38c8416e18f4e6eb8b13312eda4240c7681f1839: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1523"/><div sID="gen2042" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1523"/><hi type="bold">5-7. How goodly are thy tents, ... O Israel!--</hi>a fine burst of admiration, expressed in highly poetical strains. All travellers describe the beauty which the circular area of Bedouin tents impart to the desert. How impressive, then, must have been the view, as seen from the heights of Abarim, of the immense camp of Israel extended over the subjacent plains. <div eID="gen2042" type="x-p"/>
entries.945ed46f243059b06c93b40fadcce6ec453f1629: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1526"/><div sID="gen2046" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1526"/><hi type="bold">10-14. Balak's anger was kindled against Balaam, and he smote his hands together--</hi>The "smiting of the hands together" is, among Oriental people, an indication of the most violent rage (see <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.17">Eze 21:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.13">22:13</reference>) and ignominious dismissal. <div eID="gen2046" type="x-p"/>
entries.3664d9a7ed3d2b6272dfd5cbb1310292b7c5bdbc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1527"/><div sID="gen2047" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1527"/><hi type="bold">15. he took his parable--</hi>or prophecy, uttered in a poetical style. <div eID="gen2047" type="x-p"/>
entries.d123dd3125019e50cbfbc3f814ad7206ab70705d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1528"/><div sID="gen2048" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1528"/><hi type="bold">17. I shall see him--</hi>rather, "I do see" or "I have seen him"--a prophetic sight, like that of Abraham (<reference osisRef="John.8.56">Joh 8:56</reference>).<div eID="gen2048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2049" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">him--</hi>that is, Israel.<div eID="gen2049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2050" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel--</hi>This imagery, in the hieroglyphic language of the East, denotes some eminent ruler--primarily David; but secondarily and pre-eminently, the Messiah (see on <reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Ge 49:10</reference>).<div eID="gen2050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2051" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">corners--</hi>border, often used for a whole country (<reference osisRef="Exod.8.2">Ex 8:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.74.17">Psa 74:17</reference>).<div eID="gen2051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2052" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">children of Sheth--</hi>some prince of Moab; or, according to some, "the children of the East." <div eID="gen2052" type="x-p"/>
entries.1091994cef1563d3c354c98879e4728b96d5c45f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1529"/><div sID="gen2053" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1529"/><hi type="bold">18. Edom shall be a possession--</hi>This prophecy was accomplished by David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.14">2Sa 8:14</reference>).<div eID="gen2053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2054" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Seir--</hi>seen in the south, and poetically used for Edom. The double conquest of Moab and Edom is alluded to (<reference osisRef="Ps.60.8">Psa 60:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.108.9">108:9</reference>). <div eID="gen2054" type="x-p"/>
entries.05a538ce069d21a230c9be5f518b7a59c4b46725: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1530"/><div sID="gen2055" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1530"/><hi type="bold">19. Out of Jacob shall come he that shall have dominion--</hi>David, and particularly Christ.<div eID="gen2055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2056" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that remaineth of the city--</hi>those who flee from the field to fortified places (<reference osisRef="Ps.60.9">Psa 60:9</reference>). <div eID="gen2056" type="x-p"/>
entries.b785a6a33976b621b50047ac71bd7646a1fdb2d6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1531"/><div sID="gen2057" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1531"/><hi type="bold">20. Amalek ... his latter end shall be that he perish for ever--</hi>Their territory was seen at the remote extremity of the desert. (See on <reference osisRef="Exod.17.13">Ex 17:13</reference>; also <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.1-1Sam.15.35">1Sa 15:1-35</reference>). <div eID="gen2057" type="x-p"/>
entries.401dce0f47945051b815c1e6e1ffdf50595cd217: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1532"/><div sID="gen2058" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1532"/><hi type="bold">21. Kenites ... nest in a rock--</hi>Though securely established among the clefts in the high rocks of En-gedi towards the west, they should be gradually reduced by a succession of enemies till the Assyrian invader carried them into captivity (<reference osisRef="Judg.1.16">Jud 1:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.11">4:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.17">16, 17</reference>; also <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.29">2Ki 15:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.6">17:6</reference>). <div eID="gen2058" type="x-p"/>
entries.17d6762d83ba0154c678a730dd3939ed95f5b91d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1533"/><div sID="gen2059" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1533"/><hi type="bold">23. who shall live when God doeth this!--</hi>Few shall escape the desolation that shall send a Nebuchadnezzar to scourge all those regions. <div eID="gen2059" type="x-p"/>
entries.71d4ae172c11fcd8c7594d24515d9ae11416a2a5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1534"/><div sID="gen2060" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1534"/><hi type="bold">24. Chittim--</hi>the countries lying on the Mediterranean, particularly Greece and Italy (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.29">Da 11:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.30">30</reference>). The Assyrians were themselves to be overthrown--first, by the Greeks under Alexander the Great and his successors; secondly, by the Romans.<div eID="gen2060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2061" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Eber--</hi>the posterity of the Hebrews (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.24">Ge 10:24</reference>).<div eID="gen2061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2062" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he also shall perish--</hi>that is, the conqueror of Asher and Eber, namely, the Greek and Roman empires. <div eID="gen2062" type="x-p"/>
entries.88140698d5d02a9c4bfc27c1b4c51b6fdea70ab5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1535"/><div sID="gen2063" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1535"/><hi type="bold">25. Balaam rose up, and went ... to his place--</hi>Mesopotamia, to which, however, he did not return. (See on <reference osisRef="Num.31.8">Nu 31:8</reference>). <chapter eID="Num.24"/>

entries.dc82110a7a64a19812ce4cc301494281be5b7a30: <div eID="gen5975" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen5976" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5977" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5977" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5976" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5978" type="x-p"/> Balaam, finding that God was determined to bless Israel, seeks no longer for enchantments, <reference osisRef="Num.24.1">Num 24:1</reference>. The Spirit of God coming upon him, he delivers a most important prophetic parable, <reference osisRef="Num.24.2-Num.24.9">Num 24:2-9</reference>. Balak's anger is kindled against him, and he commands him to depart to his own country, <reference osisRef="Num.24.10">Num 24:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.24.11">Num 24:11</reference>. Balaam vindicates his conduct, <reference osisRef="Num.24.12">Num 24:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.24.13">Num 24:13</reference>; and delivers a prophecy relative to the future destruction of Moab by the Israelites, <reference osisRef="Num.24.14-Num.24.17">Num 24:14-17</reference>; also of Edom, <reference osisRef="Num.24.18">Num 24:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.24.19">Num 24:19</reference>; of the Amalekites, <reference osisRef="Num.24.20">Num 24:20</reference>; and of the Kenites, <reference osisRef="Num.24.21">Num 24:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.24.22">Num 24:22</reference>. Predicts also the destruction of Asshur and Eber, by the naval power of Chittim, which should afterwards be itself destroyed, <reference osisRef="Num.24.23">Num 24:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.24.24">Num 24:24</reference>. Balaam and Balak separate, <reference osisRef="Num.24.25">Num 24:25</reference>. <div eID="gen5978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5979" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen5979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5980" type="x-p"/> He went not, as at other times, to seek for enchantments - We have already had occasion to observe that the proper meaning of the word נחש nachash is not easily ascertained; see <reference osisRef="Num.21.9">Num 21:9</reference> (note), and <reference osisRef="Gen.3.1">Gen 3:1</reference> (note). Here the plural נחשים nechashim is rendered enchantments; but it probably means no more than the knowledge of future events. When Balaam saw that it pleased God to bless Israel, he therefore thought it unnecessary to apply for any farther prophetic declarations of God's will as he had done before, for he could safely infer every good to this people, from the evident disposition of God towards them.
entries.2dedbeb09a1b098e9535334c9c9f6f1735599fd9: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen5980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5981" type="x-p"/> The Spirit of God came upon him - This Divine afflatus he had not expected on the present occasion, but God had not yet declared the whole of his will.
entries.bf5b35b0c354af6729b19c3571dfcdd467f8a7c5: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen5981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5982" type="x-p"/> He took up his parable - His prophetic declaration couched in highly poetic terms, and in regular metre, as the preceding were. <div eID="gen5982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5983" type="x-p"/> The man whose eyes are open - I believe the original שתם shethum, should be translated shut, not open; for in the next verse, where the opening of his eyes is mentioned, a widely different word is used, גלה galah, which signifies to open or reveal. At first the eyes of Balaam were shut, and so closely too that he could not see the angel who withstood him, till God opened his eyes; nor could he see the gracious intentions of God towards Israel, till the eyes of his understanding were opened by the powers of the Divine Spirit. This therefore he mentions, we may suppose, with humility and gratitude, and to the credit of the prophecy which he is now about to deliver, that the Moabites may receive it as the word of God, which must be fulfilled in due season. His words, in their meaning, are similar to those of the blind man in the Gospel: "Once I was blind, but now I see."
entries.439a56f55fcaaffbd36fcb30af5ab3c927e69c57: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen5983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5984" type="x-p"/> Falling into a trance - There is no indication in the Hebrew that he fell into a trance; these words are added by our translators, but they are not in the original. נפל nophel is the only word used, and simply signifies falling, or falling down, perhaps in this instance by way of religious prostration.
entries.da49f655a43999e61aa367e5c0633154f640a08e: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen5984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5985" type="x-p"/> Lign aloes which the Lord hath planted - Or, as the tents which the Lord hath pitched; for it is the same word, אהלים ohalim, which is used in the 5th verse. But from other parts of Scripture we find that the word also signifies a species of tree, called by some the sandal tree, and by others the lignum or wood aloes. This tree is described as being eight or ten feet high, with very large leaves growing at the top; and it is supposed that a forest of those at some distance must bear some resemblance to a numerous encampment. As the word comes from the root אהל ahal, which signifies to spread or branch out, and therefore is applied to tents, because of their being extended or spread out on the ground; so when it is applied to trees it must necessarily mean such as were remarkable for their widely-extended branches; but what the particular species is, cannot be satisfactorily ascertained. By the Lord's planting are probably meant such trees as grow independently of the cultivation of man - Nullis hominum cogentibus; or, as Virgil expresses it, <div eID="gen5985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5986" type="x-p"/> Sponte sua quae se tollunt in luminis oras. <div eID="gen5986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5987" type="x-p"/> Virg., Geor. ii., 47. "Such as sprung up, spontaneously into the regions of light." <div eID="gen5987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5988" type="x-p"/> As cedar trees - Gabriel Sionita, a very learned Syrian Maronite, who assisted in editing the Paris Polyglot, a man worthy of all credit, thus describes the cedars of Mount Lebanon, which he had examined on the spot: - "The cedar grows on the most elevated part of the mountain, is taller than the pine, and so thick that five men together could scarcely fathom one. It shoots out its branches at ten or twelve feet from the ground; they are large, and distant from each other, and are perpetually green. The cedar distils a kind of gum, to which different effects are attributed. The wood of it is of a brown color, very solid, and incorruptible if preserved from wet. It bears a small apple, like to that of the pine." <div eID="gen5988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5989" type="x-p"/> Deuteronomy la Roque relates some curious particulars concerning this tree, which he learned from the Maronites of Mount Libanus: "The branches grow in parallel rows round the tree, but lessen gradually from the bottom to the top, shooting out parallel to the horizon, so that the tree is, in appearance, similar to a cone. As the snows, which fall in vast quantities on this mountain, must necessarily, by their weight on such a vast surface, break down these branches, nature, or rather the God of nature, has so ordered it, that at the approach of winter, and during the snowy season, the branches erect themselves, and cling close to the body of the tree, and thus prevent any quantity of snow from lodging on them." <div eID="gen5989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5990" type="x-p"/> Mr. Maundrell, who visited Mount Libanus in 1697, gives the following description of the cedars still growing there: - "These noble trees grow among the snow, near the highest part of Lebanon, and are remarkable, as well for their own age and largeness as for those frequent allusions to them in the word of God. Some of them are very old, and of a prodigious bulk; others younger, and of a smaller size. Of the former I could reckon only sixteen, but the latter are very numerous. I measured one of the largest, and found it twelve yards and six inches in girt, and yet sound, and thirty-seven yards in the spread of its branches. At about five or six yards from the ground it was divided into five limbs, each of which was equal to a great tree." - Journey from Aleppo to Jerusalem, p. 142.
entries.42449e72875c8106b5d6cdea11199bc8001db3fd: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen5990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5991" type="x-p"/> He shall pour the water out of his buckets, etc. - Here is a very plain allusion to their method of raising water in different parts of the East. By the well a tall pole is erected, which serves as a fulcrum to a very long lever, to the smaller end of which a bucket is appended. On the opposite end, which is much larger, are many notches cut in the wood, which serve as steps for a man, whose business it is to climb up to the fulcrum, in order to lower the bucket into the well, which, when filled, he raises by walking back on the opposite arm, till his weight brings the bucket above the well's mouth: a person standing by the well empties the bucket into a trench, which communicates with the ground intended to be watered. <div eID="gen5991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5992" type="x-p"/> His seed shall be in many waters - Another simple allusion to the sowing of rice. The ground must not only be well watered, but flooded, in order to serve for the proper growth of this grain. The rice that was sown in many waters must be the most fruitful. By an elegant and chaste metaphor all this is applied to the procreation of a numerous posterity. <div eID="gen5992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5993" type="x-p"/> His king shall be higher than Agag - This name is supposed to have been as common to all the Amalekitish kings as Pharaoh was to those of Egypt. But several critics, with the Septuagint, suppose that a small change has taken place here in the original word, and that instead of מאגג meagag, than Agag, we should read מגוג miggog, than Gog. As Gog in Scripture seems to mean the enemies of God's people, then the promise here may imply that the true worshippers of the Most High shall ultimately have dominion over all their enemies.
entries.0c4a53e63c769e7f90b117f66879e4afaf56eeec: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen5993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5994" type="x-p"/> God brought him forth out of Egypt - They were neither expelled thence, nor came voluntarily away. God alone, with a high hand and uplifted arm, brought them forth. Concerning the unicorn, see <reference osisRef="Num.23.22">Num 23:22</reference> (note).
entries.1487b5dc3e1cd0477747e477d94e44853836a730: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen5994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5995" type="x-p"/> He couched, he lay down as a lion, etc. - See the original terms explained <reference osisRef="Num.23.24">Num 23:24</reference> (note). <div eID="gen5995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5996" type="x-p"/> These oracles, delivered by Balaam, are evident prophecies of the victories which the Israelites should gain over their enemies, and of their firm possession of the promised land. They may also refer to the great victories to be obtained by the Lord Jesus Christ, that Lion of the tribe of Judah, over sin, death, and Satan, the grand enemies of the human race; and to that most numerous posterity of spiritual children which should be begotten by the preaching of the Gospel.
entries.85d98416d9345080dd0097b121215b0f95af7529: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen5996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5997" type="x-p"/> Lo, the Lord hath kept thee back from honor - A bitter and impious sarcasm. "Hadst thou cursed this people, I would have promoted thee to great honor; but thou hast chosen to follow the directions of Jehovah rather than mine, and what will he do for thee?"
entries.92c62d15cfeb595da09bb15e9800bff0a932d0c1: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen5997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5998" type="x-p"/> The man whose eyes are open - See on <reference osisRef="Num.24.3">Num 24:3</reference> (note). It seems strange that our version should have fallen into such a mistake as to render שתם shethum, open, which it does not signify, when the very sound of the word expresses the sense. The Vulgate has very properly preserved the true meaning, by rendering the clause cujus obturatus est oculus, he whose eyes are shut. The Targum first paraphrased the passage falsely, and most of the versions followed it.
entries.8a5eda187b5f5ee9877dfd788d3c73fe0630221e: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen5998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5999" type="x-p"/> I shall see him, but not now - Or, I shall see him, but he is not now. I shall behold him, but not nigh - I shall have a full view of him, but the time is yet distant. That is, The person of whom I am now prophesying does not at present exist among these Israelites, nor shall he appear in this generation. There shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel - a person eminent for wisdom, and formidable for strength and power, shall arise as king among this people. He shall smite the corners of Moab - he shall bring the Moabites perfectly under subjection; (See <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.2">2Sam 8:2</reference>); and destroy all the children of Sheth. The original word קרקר karkar, from קרה karah, to meet, associate, join, blend, and the like, is variously translated; vastabit, he shall waste, Vulgate - προνομευσει, shall prey on, Sept - ישלוט yishlot, shall rule over, Targum - Shall shake, Arabic - barbend, shall put a yoke on, Pers - Shall unwall, Ainsworth, etc., etc. <div eID="gen5999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6000" type="x-p"/> The Targum of Onkelos translates the whole passage thus: "I shall see him, but not now: I shall behold him, but he is not near. When a king shall arise from the house of Jacob, and the Messiah be anointed from the house of Israel, he shall slay the princes of Moab, and rule over all the children of men." <div eID="gen6000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6001" type="x-p"/> The Jerusalem Targum is a little different: "A king shall arise from the house of Jacob, a redeemer and governor from the house of Israel, who shall slay the chiefs of the Moabites, and empty out and destroy all the children of the East." <div eID="gen6001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6002" type="x-p"/> Rabbi Moses ben Maimon has, in my opinion, perfectly hit the meaning of the prophecy in the following paraphrase of the text: "I shall see him, but not now. This is David - I shall behold him, but not nigh. This is the king Messiah - A Star shall come out of Jacob. This is David - And a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel. This is the king Messiah - And shall smite the corners of Moab. This is David, (as it is written, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.2">2Sam 8:2</reference> : And he smote Moab, casting them down to the ground) - And shall destroy all the children of Sheth. This is the king Messiah, of whom it is written, (<reference osisRef="Psa.72.8">Psa 72:8</reference>), He shall have dominion from sea to sea."
entries.4446dfa4cd6fe70302c1c9d04aa3c27ac6223cc9: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen6002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6003" type="x-p"/> And Edom shall be a possession - That is, to David: as it is said: "And all they of Edom became David's servants;" <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.14">2Sam 8:14</reference>. <div eID="gen6003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6004" type="x-p"/> Seir also shall be a possession - That is, unto the king Messiah; as it is said: "And saviours shall come upon Mount Zion to judge the Mount of Esau; and the kingdom shall be the Lord's;" <reference osisRef="Oba.1.21">Oba 1:21</reference>. See Ainsworth.
entries.c9b81007a31688fb44060da97622eb6f2127c11b: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen6004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6005" type="x-p"/> Out of Jacob shall come, etc. - This is supposed to refer to Christ, because of what is said <reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Gen 49:10</reference>. <div eID="gen6005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6006" type="x-p"/> It is exceedingly difficult to fix the true sense of this prophecy in all its particulars. Probably the star, <reference osisRef="Num.24.17">Num 24:17</reference>, is only an emblem of kingly power. Among the Egyptians a star is said to have been the symbol of the Divine Being. The scepter refers to the kingly power in exercise. The corners or outskirts may mean the petty Moabitish governments, as the Chaldee has understood the term. If karkar, which we translate utterly destroy, be not the name of a place here, as it is in <reference osisRef="Jdg.8.10">Jdg 8:10</reference>, (which is not very likely), it may be taken in one of those senses assigned to it, (see on <reference osisRef="Num.24.17">Num 24:17</reference> (note)), and signify the blending together the children of Sheth, that is, all the inhabitants of the earth; for so the children of Sheth must necessarily be understood, unless we consider it here as meaning some king of the Moabites, according to Grotius, or a city on the borders of Moab, according to Rabbi Nathan. As neither Israel nor the Messiah ever destroyed all the children of men, we must (in order to leave the children of Sheth what they are generally understood to be, all the inhabitants of the world) understand the whole as a prophecy of the final universal sway of the scepter of Christ, when the middle wall of partition shall be broken down, and the Jews and Gentiles become one united, blended fold, under one shepherd and bishop of their souls. <div eID="gen6006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6007" type="x-p"/> I cannot think that the meteoric star which guided the wise men of the east to Bethlehem can be intended here; nor do I think that Peter refers to this prophecy when he calls Christ the day star, <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.19">2Pet 1:19</reference>; nor that <reference osisRef="Rev.2.28">Rev 2:28</reference>, where Christ is called the morning star, nor <reference osisRef="Rev.22.16">Rev 22:16</reference>, where he is called the bright and morning star, refers at all to this prophecy of Balaam. Nor do I think that the false Christ who rose in the time of Adrian, and who called himself Barcochab, which literally signifies the son of a star, did refer to this prophecy. If he had, he must have defeated his own intention, because the Son of the star is not The Star that should arise, but at the utmost a descendant; and then, to vindicate his right to the Jewish throne, he must show that the person who was called the star, and of whom he pretended to be the son or descendant, had actually reigned before him. As the sun, moon, stars, planets, light, splendours, effulgence, day, etc., were always considered among the Asiatics as emblems of royalty, government, etc., therefore many, both men and women, had these names given to them as titles, surnames, etc. So the queen of Alexander the Great, called Roxana by the Greeks, was a Persian princess, and in her native tongue her name was Roushen, splendor. Hadassah, who became queen to Ahasuerus, in place of the repudiated Vashti, and is called Esther by Europeans in general, was called in the language of Persia Sitareh; from whence by corruption came both Esther, the Persian queen, and our word star. And to waive all farther examples, a Mohammedan prince, at first named Eesouf or Joseph, was called Roushen Akhter when he was raised to the throne, which signifies a splendid or luminous star. This prince, by a joyful reverse of fortune, was brought from a gloomy prison and exalted to the throne of Hindostan; on which account the following couplet was made, in which there is a paronomasia or play on the name Roushen Akhter; and the last line alludes to the history of the patriarch Joseph, who was brought out of prison and exalted to the highest honors in Egypt. <div eID="gen6007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6008" type="x-p"/> Roushen Akhter bood, aknoon mah shud̀ <div eID="gen6008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6009" type="x-p"/> Yousef az zendan ber amd shah shud. "He was a bright star, but is now become a moon. <div eID="gen6009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6010" type="x-p"/> Joseph is brought out of prison, and is become a glorious king."
entries.060f94ca27c89ffa4c652c716b8fe4fedd6dd871: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen6010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6011" type="x-p"/> Amalek was the first of the nations - The most ancient and most powerful of all the nations or states then within the view of Balaam; but his latter end shall be that he perish for ever, or his posterity אחריתו acharitho, shall be destroyed, or shall utterly fail. This oracle began to be fulfilled by Saul, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.7">1Sam 15:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.8">1Sam 15:8</reference>, who overthrew the Amalekites, and took their king, Agag, prisoner. Afterwards they were nearly destroyed by David, <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.8">1Sam 27:8</reference>, and they were finally exterminated by the sons of Simeon in the days of Hezekiah, <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.41-1Chr.4.43">1Chr 4:41-43</reference>; since that time they have ceased to exist as a people, and now no vestige of them remains on the face of the earth; so completely is their posterity cut off, according to this prophecy. The marginal reading does not appear to give the proper sense.
entries.3bbadcb6131124d01fe4e85f4160db56f2144937: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen6011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6012" type="x-p"/> He looked on the Kenites - Commentators are not well agreed who the Kenites were. Dr. Dodd's opinion is, I think, nearest to the truth. Jethro, the father-in-law of Moses, is called a priest or prince of Midian, <reference osisRef="Exo.3.1">Exo 3:1</reference>, and in <reference osisRef="Jdg.1.16">Jdg 1:16</reference> he is called a Kenite; we may infer, therefore, says he, that the Kenites and the Midianites were the same, or at least that the Kenites and the Midianites were confederate tribes. Some of these we learn from Judges 1, followed the Israelites, others abode still among the Midianites and Amalekites. When Saul destroyed the latter, we find he had no commission against the Kenites, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.6">1Sam 15:6</reference>, for it appears that they were then a small and inconsiderable people; they had doubtless been wasted, as the text says, though by what means does not appear from history. On the other hand, it may be observed that the Midianites mentioned here lived close to the Dead Sea, at a great distance from the Midian where Jethro lived, which was near Horeb. Perhaps they were a colony or tribe that had migrated from the vicinity of Mount Sinai. It seems that at this time the Kenites occupied a very strong position: Strong is thy dwelling place, and thou puttest thy nest in a rock; where there is a play on the original word קי, which signifies both a Kenite and a nest. High rocks in these countries were generally used as their strong places.
entries.2117ced29ea494e77dcff236138ce1be0671d005: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen6012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6013" type="x-p"/> Until Asshur shall carry thee away captive - The Assyrians and Babylonians who carried away captive the ten tribes, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.6">2Kgs 17:6</reference>, and the Jews into Babylon, 2 Kings 25, probably carried away the Kenites also. Indeed this seems pretty evident, as we find some Kenites mentioned among the Jews after their return from the Babylonish captivity, <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.55">1Chr 2:55</reference>.
entries.eb20bdbe2b9cd530c8867115931e37f17886596a: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen6013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6014" type="x-p"/> Who shall live when God doeth this! - There are two senses in which these words may be taken: - <div eID="gen6014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6015" type="x-p"/> 1. That the event is so distant that none then alive could possibly live to see it. <div eID="gen6015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6016" type="x-p"/> 2. That the times would be so distressing and desolating that scarcely any should be able to escape. <div eID="gen6016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6017" type="x-p"/> The words are very similar to those of our Lord, and probably are to be taken in the same sense: "Wo to them that are with child, and to them that give suck in those days."
entries.d1698473c3d6d39bc34cf6f04d339b01e7acdac8: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen6017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6018" type="x-p"/> Ships shall come from the coast of Chittim - Some think by Chittim the Romans, others the Macedonians under Alexander the Great, are meant. It is certain that the Romans did conquer the Assyrians, including all the people of Syria, Mesopotamia, etc., but Calmet strongly contends that by Chittim Macedonia is meant, and that the prophecy refers to the conquests of Alexander. Chittim was one of the sons of Javan, the son of Japheth, the son of Noah, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.4">Gen 10:4</reference>; and his posterity, according to Josephus, Antiq., 1. iii., c. 22, settled in Cilicia, Macedonia, Cyprus, and Italy also; and therefore, says Mr. Ainsworth, the prophecy may imply both the troubles that befell the Assyrians and Jews by the Greeks and Seleucidae, in the troublous days of Antiochus. <div eID="gen6018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6019" type="x-p"/> And shall afflict Eber - Probably not the Hebrews, as some think, but the people on the other side the Euphrates, from עבר abar, to pass over, go beyond; all which people were discomfited, and their empire destroyed by Alexander the Great.
entries.25c0633557b0ce147965cbd3c0679e7d9178b56e: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen6019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6020" type="x-p"/> And Balaam - returned to his place - Intended to have gone to Mesopotamia, his native country, (see <reference osisRef="Deu.23.4">Deu 23:4</reference>), but seems to have settled among the Midianites, where he was slain by the Israelites; see <reference osisRef="Num.31.8">Num 31:8</reference>. <div eID="gen6020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6021" type="x-p"/> Though the notes in the preceding chapters have been extended to a considerable length, yet a few additional remarks may be necessary: the reader's attention is earnestly requested to the following propositions: - <div eID="gen6021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6022" type="x-p"/> 1. It appears sufficiently evident from the preceding account that Balaam knew and worshipped the true God. <div eID="gen6022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6023" type="x-p"/> 2. That he had been a true prophet, and appears to have been in the habit of receiving oracles from God. <div eID="gen6023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6024" type="x-p"/> 3. That he practiced some illicit branches of knowledge, or was reputed by the Moabites as a sorcerer, probably because of the high reputation he had for wisdom; and we know that even in our own country, in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, persons who excelled their contemporaries in wisdom were reputed as magicians. <div eID="gen6024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6025" type="x-p"/> 4. That though he was a believer in the true God, yet he was covetous; he loved the wages of unrighteousness. <div eID="gen6025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6026" type="x-p"/> 5. That it does not appear that in the case before us he wished to curse Israel when he found they were the servants of the true God. <div eID="gen6026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6027" type="x-p"/> 6. That it is possible he did not know this at first. Balak told him that there was a numerous people come out of Egypt; and as marauders, wandering hordes, freebooters, etc., were frequent in those days, he might take them at first for such spoilers, and the more readily go at Balak's request to consult God concerning them. <div eID="gen6027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6028" type="x-p"/> 7. That so conscientiously did he act in the whole business, that as soon as he found it displeased God he cheerfully offered to return; and did not advance till he had not only the permission, but the authority of God to proceed. <div eID="gen6028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6029" type="x-p"/> 8. That when he came in view of the Israelitish camp he did not attempt to make use of any means of sorcery, evocation of spirits, necromantic spells, etc., to accomplish the wish of Balak. <div eID="gen6029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6030" type="x-p"/> 9. That he did seek to find out the will of the true God, by using those means which God himself had prescribed, viz., supplication and prayer, and the sacrifice of the clean beasts. <div eID="gen6030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6031" type="x-p"/> 10. That though he knew it would greatly displease Balak, yet he most faithfully and firmly told him all that God said on every occasion. <div eID="gen6031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6032" type="x-p"/> 11. That notwithstanding his allowed covetous disposition, yet he refused all promised honors and proffered rewards, even of the most extensive kind, to induce him to act in any respect contrary to the declared will of God. <div eID="gen6032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6033" type="x-p"/> 12. That God on this occasion communicated to him some of the most extraordinary prophetic influences ever conferred on man. <div eID="gen6033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6034" type="x-p"/> 13. That his prophecies are, upon the whole, clear and pointed, and have been fulfilled in the most remarkable manner, and furnish a very strong argument in proof of Divine revelation. <div eID="gen6034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6035" type="x-p"/> 14. That notwithstanding the wicked counsel given to the Midianites, the effects of which are mentioned in the following chapter, on which account he probably lost his life, (<reference osisRef="Num.31.8">Num 31:8</reference>), the badness of this man's character has been very far overrated; and that it does not appear that he was either a hypocrite, false prophet, or a sorcerer in the common acceptation of the term, and that he risked even life itself in following and fulfilling the will of the Lord! <div eID="gen6035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6036" type="x-p"/> 15. That though it is expressly asserted, <reference osisRef="Num.31.16">Num 31:16</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Rev.2.14">Rev 2:14</reference>, that Israel's committing whoredom with the daughters of Moab was brought about by the evil counsel given by Balaam to cast this stumbling-block in their way, yet it does not appear from the text that he had those most criminal intentions which are generally attributed to him; for as we have already seen so much good in this man's character, and that this, and his love of money (and who thinks this a sin?) are almost the only blots in it, it must certainly be consistent with candour and charity to suggest a method of removing at least some part of this blame. <div eID="gen6036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6037" type="x-p"/> 16. I would therefore simply say that the counsel given by Balaam to Balak might have been "to form alliances with this people, especially through the medium of matrimonial connections; and seeing they could not conquer them, to endeavor to make them their friends." Now, though this might not be designed by Balaam to bring them into a snare, yet it was a bad doctrine, as it led to the corruption of the holy seed, and to an unequal yoking with unbelievers; which, though even in a matrimonial way, is as contrary to sound policy as to the word of God. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Num.25.3">Num 25:3</reference> and <reference osisRef="Num.25.6">Num 25:6</reference> (note). <div eID="gen6037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6038" type="x-p"/> 17. That it was the Moabitish women, not Balaam, that called the people to the sacrifice of their gods; and it argued great degeneracy and iniquity in the hearts of the people on so slight an invitation to join so suddenly so impure a worship, and so speedily to cast off the whole form of godliness, with every portion of the fear of the Almighty; therefore the high blame rests ultimately with themselves.  <chapter eID="Num.24"/> <div eID="gen6038" type="x-p"/>

entries.515ac405ded6a9f9cfff0c8a1531827f1c94b163: The <hi type="italic">third</hi> saying. - Num 24:1 and Num 24:2. From the two revelations which he had received before, Balaam, saw, i.e., perceived, that it pleased Jehovah to bless Israel. This induced him not to go out for auguries, as on the previous occasions. כּפעם־בּפעם, “as time after time,” i.e., as at former times (Num 23:3 and Num 23:15). He therefore turned his face to the desert, i.e., to the steppes of Moab, where Israel was encamped (Num 22:1). And when he lifted up his eyes, “<hi type="italic">he saw Israel encamping according to its tribes; and the Spirit of God came over him</hi>.” The impression made upon him by the sight of the tribes of Israel, served as the subjective preparation for the reception of the Spirit of God to inspire him. Of both the earlier utterances it is stated that “Jehovah put a word into his mouth” (Num 23:5 and Num 23:16); but of this third it is affirmed that “the Spirit of God came over him.” The former were communicated to him, when he went out for a divine revelation, without his being thrown into an ecstatic state; he heard the voice of God within him telling him what he was to say. But this time, like the prophets in their prophesyings, he was placed by the Spirit of God in a state of ecstatic sight; so that, with his eyes closed as in clairvoyance, he saw the substance of the revelation from God with his inward mental eye, which had been opened by the Spirit of God. Thus not only does he himself describe his own condition in Num 24:3 and Num 24:4, but his description is in harmony with the announcement itself, which is manifestly the result both in form and substance of the intuition effected within him by the Spirit of God. <div eID="gen1949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1950" type="x-p"/> Num 24:3 and Num 24:4 contain the preface to the prophecy: “<hi type="italic">The divine saying of Balaam the son of Beor, the divine saying of the man with closed eye, the divine saying of the hearer of divine words, who sees the vision of the Almighty, falling down and with opened eyes</hi>.” For the participial noun נאם the meaning divine saying (<hi type="italic">effatum</hi>, not <hi type="italic">inspiratum</hi>, <hi type="italic">Domini</hi>) is undoubtedly established by the expression יהוה נאם, which recurs in Num 14:28 and <reference osisRef="Gen.22.16">Gen 22:16</reference>, and is of constant use in the predictions of the prophets; and this applies even to the few passages where a human author is mentioned instead of Jehovah, such as Num 24:3, Num 24:4, and Num 24:15, Num 24:16; also <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.1">2Sa 23:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.30.1">Pro 30:1</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Ps.36.2">Psa 36:2</reference>, where a נאם is ascribed to the personified wickedness. Hence, when Balaam calls the following prophecy a נאם, this is done for the purpose of designating it as a divine revelation received from the Spirit of God. He had received it, and now proclaimed it as a man העין שׁתם, with closed eye. שׁתם does not mean to open, a meaning in support of which only one passage of the <hi type="italic">Mishnah</hi> can be adduced, but to close, like סתם in <reference osisRef="Dan.8.26">Dan 8:26</reference>, and שׁתם in <reference osisRef="Lam.3.8">Lam 3:8</reference>, with the שׁ softened into ס or   שׂ (see <hi type="italic">Roediger</hi> in <hi type="italic">Ges</hi>. thes., and <hi type="italic">Dietrich's</hi> Hebrew Lexicon). “Balaam describes himself as the man with closed eye with reference to his state of ecstasy, in which the closing of the outer senses went hand in hand with the opening of the inner” (Hengstenberg). The cessation of all perception by means of the outer senses, so far as self-conscious reflection is concerned, was a feature that was common to both the vision and the dream, the two forms in which the prophetic gift manifested itself (Num 12:6), and followed from the very nature of the inward intuition. In the case of prophets whose spiritual life was far advanced, inspiration might take place without any closing of the outward senses. But upon men like Balaam, whose inner religious life was still very impure and undeveloped, the Spirit of God could only operate by closing their outward senses to impressions from the lower earthly world, and raising them up to visions of the higher and spiritual world.<note placement="foot">Hence, as Hengstenberg observes (Balaam, p. 449), we have to picture Balaam as giving utterance to his prophecies with the eyes of his body closed; though we cannot argue from the fact of his being in this condition, that an Isaiah would be in precisely the same. Compare the instructive information concerning analogous phenomena in the sphere of natural mantik and ecstasy in Hengstenberg (pp. 449ff.), and <hi type="italic">Tholuck’s Propheten</hi>, pp. 49ff.</note> <div eID="gen1950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1951" type="x-p"/> What Balaam heard in this ecstatic condition was אל אמרי, the sayings of God, and what he saw שׁדּי מחזה, the vision of the Almighty. The Spirit of God came upon him with such power that he fell down (נפל), like Saul in <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.24">1Sa 19:24</reference>; not merely “prostrating himself with reverential awe at seeing and hearing the things of God” (<hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>), but thrown to the ground by the Spirit of God, who “came like an armed man upon the seer,” and that in such a way that as he fell his (spirit’s) eyes were opened. This introduction to his prophecy is not an utterance of boasting vanity; but, as <hi type="italic">Calvin</hi> correctly observes, “the whole preface has no other tendency than to prove that he was a true prophet of God, and had received the blessing which he uttered from a celestial oracle.” <div eID="gen1951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1952" type="x-p"/> The blessing itself in Num 24:5. contains two thoughts: (1) the glorious prosperity of Israel, and the exaltation of its kingdom (Num 24:5-7); (2) the terrible power, so fatal to all its foes, of the people which was set to be a curse or a blessing to all the nations (Num 24:8, Num 24:9).
entries.f1f1cdfe43b3e31c383a33e47a89e97931ac2ac8: Num 24:5-6 <div eID="gen1952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1953" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">How beautiful are thy tents, O Jacob! thy dwellings, O Israel! Like valleys are they spread out, like gardens by the stream, like aloes which Jehovah has planted, like cedars by the waters. Water will flow out of his buckets, and his seed is by many waters. And loftier than Agag be his king, and his kingdom will be exalted</hi>.” What Balaam had seen before his ecstasy with his bodily eyes, formed the substratum for his inward vision, in which the dwellings of Israel came before his mental eye adorned with the richest blessing from the Lord. The description starts, it is true, from the time then present, but it embraces the whole future of Israel. In the blessed land of Canaan the dwellings of Israel will spread out like valleys. נחלים does not mean brooks here, but valleys watered by brooks. נטּה, to extend oneself, to stretch or spread out far and wide. Yea, “like gardens by the stream,” which are still more lovely than the grassy and flowery valleys with brooks. This thought is carried out still further in the two following figures. אהלים are aloe-trees, which grow in the East Indies, in Siam, in Cochin China, and upon the Moluccas, and from which the aloe-wood was obtained, that was so highly valued in the preparation of incense, on account of its fragrance. As the aloes were valued for their fragrant smell, so the cedars were valued on account of their lofty and luxuriant growth, and the durability of their wood. The predicate, “which Jehovah hath planted,” corresponds, so far as the actual meaning is concerned, to מים עלי, “by water;” for this was “an expression used to designate trees that, on account of their peculiar excellence, were superior to ordinary trees” (<hi type="italic">Calvin</hi>; cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.104.16">Psa 104:16</reference>).
entries.31b53c1f9f6bf89ded3a6f0bcc37d8dd4c5c4581: Num 24:7 <div eID="gen1953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1954" type="x-p"/> And not only its dwellings, but Israel itself would also prosper abundantly. It would have an abundance of water, that leading source of all blessing and prosperity in the burning East. The nation is personified as a man carrying two pails overflowing with water. דּליו is the dual דּליים.
